title: How the Mind Generates Reality, a First Look
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads the opening of lesson four in Seven and a Half Lessons About the Brain, "Your brain predicts (almost) everything you do," after a vaccine appointment cuts into preparation time. A drafted Rhodesian soldier aims at a line of guerrillas carrying an AK-47 until a buddy whispers that it is just a boy leading cows with a herding stick. Nomon connects this constructed, predictive seeing to the Yogachara storehouse consciousness, where seeds of fear or patience wait to sprout, and promises a fuller treatment next week. The evening closes with congratulations to Corinne and Richard, who received jukai over Zoom, and an update on the campaign committee.
topics: "Seven and a Half Lessons about the Brain"

sentences.text: **Nomon Tim Burnett:** Good evening everybody, good to see you.
First I want to say a little bit about my afternoon.

I was sitting down to organize the talk this afternoon, and then the phone rang and it was the county health department telling me that there was a second dose of Pfizer vaccine available for me right now.
I had a lead on a dose tomorrow that might have worked, but she said, "If I were you, I'd go."
So I went.
Anyway, I didn't really have any time to prepare the talk.
So I'll just tell you a little bit about where we're going and really prepare next week, because this next chapter in the book, *Seven and a Half Lessons About the Brain*, is the thing, I think.
It was in the article in the New York Times that I first found out about this author and this book.
It's about how the brain, in this view, right, they're talking about the brain and in our Buddhist view the mind, really does generate reality.
And this chapter, I think, is just stunningly cognizant and supportive of the mind-only schools, of which the Yogachara school that we're also looking at a little bit is a part.

So what I want to do is just read the opening section of the chapter, say just a couple of things, and give myself till next week to really organize and weave it together, because I think it's quite amazing.
And not just because super cool science and Buddhism are lining up, which is not always true, you know, sometimes they do, sometimes they don't.
It's also because I think this material and this way of understanding reality is pointing out basically that in very fundamental ways we misunderstand our experience and misunderstand reality.

And this understanding, I believe, like Buddhist understanding, leads to more flexibility, more patience, more kindness, more understanding, especially in between us humans, and also supports a more effective and wise approach to our own growth and healing.
Because how can we really operate well or try to change anything if our notion about what's actually happening every moment is wrong in some fundamental ways?
It also makes some really interesting suggestions about time, and that our notion of time and even our notion of the present moment is a little bit off.
So I think it's just fascinating and amazing, and I'm putting all my eggs in the basket of this one book.

But as I said before, she seems to be a very well credentialed and respected neuroscientist, and there's a million references in the back, so I'm assuming that it is really an authoritative source, if simplified.
But in this respect the big picture isn't simplified, it's all the details that are simplified.
So here's the beginning of the chapter that so caught my attention when it showed up in the article in the Times.
The title of lesson four, the fifth chapter, also kind of says it all: "Your brain predicts almost everything you do," with the "almost" in parentheses.
So there's a big idea in here about prediction.

Not only is what we're experiencing a function of the brain, a function of the mind, and not exactly the direct experience we think it is, but this prediction business has to do with time being a little shifted from what we think it is.
So it's a lot, and I'm looking forward to spending a couple of weeks on it.
Now I'm grateful for the health department for slowing me down, slowing us down.
By the way, the other thing that was nice when that call came was I knew I could trust everybody to be supportive of me getting a vaccine and not having a perfect talk.
It took me, of course, a few minutes to get over my perfectionism.
But that's mine, you know, I knew that that wasn't yours.
So thank you for that.
And our song, we asked you perfect.
What a good thing.
Anyway, here's the chapter.
*A few years ago, I received an email from a man who'd served in the Rhodesian army in southern Africa in the 1970s, just before the end of apartheid.
He'd been drafted against his will, handed a uniform and a rifle in order to hunt down guerrilla fighters.
To make matters worse, before the draft, he'd been an advocate for some of the same guerrillas that he was now required to treat as enemies.
He was deep in the forest one morning, conducting practice exercises with his small squad of soldiers when he detected movement ahead of him.
With a pounding heart, he saw a line of guerrilla fighters dressed in camouflage, carrying machine guns.
Instinctively, he raised his rifle, flipped off the safety catch, and squinted down the barrel aiming at their leader who was carrying an AK-47 assault rifle.
Suddenly, he felt a hand on his shoulder.
"Don't shoot!
Don't shoot!" whispered his buddy behind him.
"It's just a boy."
He slowly lowered his rifle and looked again at the scene.*
*I was astonished by what he now saw.
A boy, perhaps 10 years old, leading a long line of cows.
And the dreaded AK-47, it was simply a hurting stick.*
The idea here is not that he was just overly freaked out or distraught or messed up in some way, but that he was in a very high stress situation, for sure.
And as we'll explore more thoroughly next week, his brain had good reason to produce the experience of seeing guerrilla fighters with an AK-47.
It's also not just that the cows kind of looked soldier-like and he mistook them, or a trick of the light.

No, the idea, and I'm quite convinced by this, is he really saw in great detail the actual image and had the actual experience of soldiers in a line with the rifles and the machine gun and everything.
A little more.
*For years afterward, the man struggled to understand this unsettling episode.
How he managed to mis-see what was right in front of his eyes and nearly kill a child.
What was wrong with his brain?
As it turns out, nothing was wrong with his brain.

It was working exactly as it should have.* [unclear: "And he was able to see what was exactly as it should have."] *Scientists used to believe that the brain's visual system operated sort of like a camera, detecting visual information out there in the world and constructing a photograph-like image in the mind.
Today we know better.
Your view of the world is no photograph.
It's a construction of your brain that is so fluid and so convincing that it appears to be accurate, except that sometimes it's not.*
I think it's worth noting there the way she said, "now we know different."
I don't know that all of us out here operating our minds and bodies and eyes do really know different, right?
I think we automatically assume that we're seeing exactly what we're seeing in real time and accurately, and that the eyes are like a window that we can see through.
Of course, when we think about it, we remember the eyes are not a window, right?
They're light detectors and detectors of color and contrast and all that.
And then our brain interprets them.
But I think we tend to think that that interpretation is happening in some sort of straight line fashion.
She says in this chapter, very convincingly, with lots of evidence, that's not the case.
It's not that the eyes aren't taking in visual information, light information.
They can be made into images by the mind.
That is also true.
But it's just one input of many.
And remember how massive this neurological web that is the brain is, right? 125 billion neurons and potentially trillions of possible patterns and arrangements and organizations.
And the point of all of it is to keep us going, right?
To keep us alive.
So in this example, it was a situation where there was a lot of threat, right?
There's a lot of threat for this guy to being alive.
And so his brain, based on prior experience, did what it should do, which was produce the right experience to keep him alive.
We could see this as a visual experience, an auditory experience, an immersive experience, and all experience, right, as not really different from feeling hungry or something.
The mind is doing what it needs, and the mind isn't exactly thinking in this way that we think of, it doesn't have agency in that way.
But the mind has evolved to respond to the unfolding of our life in intricate ways.

And not only does it sometimes create a situation that's different from what on second glance turns out to be another kind of reality, but it even does that in anticipation of what might happen, as we'll get into more carefully next week.

That's the trip out on top of the trip out: not only can we see things that aren't there, we can actually see things that aren't there before they're not there, if that makes any sense, or before they're there.

And the neurological wiring, there's a huge evolutionary advantage for it to be not just ready, but ready earlier, ready before something bad happens or before something good happens or something neutral happens.
So it's ready to respond in the best way for our well being.

And this is so triply, I think, in parallel and in agreement with the Yogachara system of understanding consciousness: although there is the monist mind, the mind that we think of as me, the mind that's doing the experiencing, in that system it's also having this deep conversation with the storehouse consciousness, with the deep impulses and wiring and conditioning that's stored away.
That really seems to translate to the neural pathways and neural patterns that have become more efficient, so they happen more often.
They're not exactly wired in a fixed way, right?
It's much more fluid, with lots of handoffs in that.

But our intricate network brain also can store a tremendous amount of stuff, a massive amount of stuff, just like this storehouse consciousness of Yogachara Buddhism can store a massive amount of stuff.
And when that stuff is activated, we are responding in a way that's heavily influenced by the emergence of all the stored conditioning.
Remember, they're thought of in that system as seeds.
So a seed of fear and a seed of needing to survive and a seed of anger or a seed of urgency are all sprouting, and that's interacting in some way with the other six consciousnesses.
But I was tending to think of that system as sort of happening on a linear time horizon, happening all at once.
Like we're seeing, hearing, feeling, thinking, and stuff's coming out of the storehouse consciousness.
So I'm interested to look more carefully at the book we're starting to study on Yogachara Buddhism to see if that's really how they think about it.

Because she seems to be saying it's even more wild than that: that the stuff from the storehouse, the stuff already encoded in the brain, is not just interacting with some kind of present moment stimuli and deciding.
It's predicting, it's operating a step before things actually happen to make us even more primed and ready for whatever happens next.

And so therefore free will, and the operation of our consciousness, and our attempt to change and grow, requires a more subtle and nuanced and longer term process, involving more like big feedback loops for ourselves, rather than trying to get it right every moment.
That also kind of fits Yogachara Buddhism, that we want to plant seeds of goodness, seeds of patience, seeds of generosity, seeds of love, to increase the chances that they then sprout later.

So the same thing here: we want to build neural pathways that are supportive of those kinds of impulses, so that the brain then predicts loving and positive and patient and wise and compassionate interactions with reality, rather than predicting fearful, angry, whatever you want to say, all the negative possible states.
So anyway, that's a little rambly because I didn't prepare, but I hope that primes the pump a little bit.
If you did get the book, and I've read this chapter, I recommend rereading.
I've read it three or four times now, and it's just blowing my mind, and maybe making new pathways in my brain, which I hope will be helpful to me.
I don't expect that I or any of us will completely drop our assumptions about reality and experience, because those are so ingrained.
I can't help thinking that I'm seeing you in the little zoom squares right now exactly as you are, and that I'm accessing my thoughts in real time and saying what I need to say.
But actually it seems there's much more subtle and weird stuff happening, you know, and weird stuff happening.
Before I finished the sentence, I've already fired off the neurons to start the next sentence, before even really knowing in my conscious awareness what that next sentence is going to be, somehow.
So I'll stop there before I just get rambly.
We could do a few song announcements too.
That's also good.
And we'll end a little early probably because of the pandemic and another dimension.

One is this happened a little while ago, I think, but I've been meaning to congratulate Corinne and Richard, who, if you look very carefully in the little tiny zoom screen, can see they're wearing rakusu.
They did jukai as part of their chaplaincy program at Paya.
So congratulations, you guys.
Done in the back, you know, somewhere.
How was that?
Did she do it?
Did she do that with you over zoom?
The end of the second year, first core training.
How did she manage to give you the rakusu through the screen?
That's amazing.
**Participant:** Yeah, that's the magic, right?
Yeah, no, we sent our raksus to the same day and then we got them back.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Okay.
You open the envelope at the right time.
What names did she offer you?
Yoko?
**Participant:** It was Bushin.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Bushin, oh, buddha-mania, Bushin.
Yoko.
Ko is like, what's the, which yo is that?
**Participant:** It's ko.
Sorry, I'm not close to the screen.
It's myo.
Myoko.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Oh, like radiant or subtle.
**Participant:** Yeah.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Okay.
Yeah, myoko.
Cool.
Well, how exciting.
**Participant:** Yeah, it was fun.
It was a really wonderful ceremony.
We were really impressed that they were able to pull it off.
You know, there were, what, how many people? 27 or something?
Yeah, something like that.
Not everyone chose to receive Jukai.
I think they're hoping that we'll meet next year before graduation and have an opportunity, but who knows?
So we decided to do it this year.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Very cool.
Congratulations.
Thank you for that.
Thank you for the observation.
Yeah, I spotted them a few weeks ago.
Seeing things.
You can't see all the mistakes.
Yeah, that's good.
That's good.
Yeah, we know they're there.
Oh, yeah.
Wonderful.
Feel free, if you want to add a congratulations, feel free to unmute and be a little more of a gathering here.
Meanwhile, we've started this year's Precepts cohort.
Met a couple of times.
I was talking to one of the participants and she was quite happy and supported and really appreciating that program.
We're very much hoping that we'll have an in-person Jukai first Saturday of November.
The students will be Toy Giel and Kevin Connor, hopefully, if they finish their sewing.
They've both been at this for a couple of years, so it'll be a sweet thing.
And they're both remote.
Kevin's now in Seattle and Toy, as you probably know, is in Laramie, Wyoming.
Both used to practice with us here in Bellingham.
Other news: the campaign committee is still slowly working away.
We're sorry we haven't gotten lots of information or news back, but it's just the nature of the thing and volunteer sangha groups as they are.
We've really been trying to read through and contemplate all the lots and lots of visioning feedback people offered and figure out the core themes in there.
We'll use those as how we present to the world once we start the active fundraising campaign, which will probably be in the fall.
So it's a measured slow thing, and hopefully we can be patient and move along carefully.
The campaign committee is meeting next week on Tuesday.
We'll try to get more clear with Thomas what exactly is coming next and get some information back out, and we'll just go along.
I've been talking to a few possible donors and we're slowly revving up and getting ready.
So we'll be thinking about that.
One of the things that the consultant really urged us to think about, which we can all start gradually thinking about, is: what can you yourself contribute?
He encouraged us to think about that.
He was like, just expect other people that, you know.

But the other thing that's been interesting is really think about friends and loved ones, even if they have no personal direct interest or experience with Buddhism or Zen, but they care about you and they care about things that you care about.
They might like to support something that matters to you, in this case the sangha's new home, whatever that turns out to be.
Later in the process, we will refine the actual physical vision as well.
But I'm really kind of impressed, and it's counterintuitive to me, just like the brain stuff, that it's really wise, I think, to not jump right to how many rooms and what size and blah, blah, blah.
Because then sometimes the tail ends up wagging the dog.
Better to really think about what are we trying to do?
What are we trying to offer?
What's our heart intention?
And then how is that expressed in a building?
That said, it's a zendo, so it'll have some stuff that we all know what it'll be.
There'll be a meditation hall, there'll be a lobby, all the stuff.
But exactly what configuration, and where in town, and how is it accessed?
How should those choices be influenced by this collective vision that we're trying to assess?
So anyway, we'll get more back out about that too.
I wanted to update you, and I think that's all I got at the moment.
Other announcements, song of things or things in your life you want to share?
All right then.
Let's chant and get to bed early.
Good for us.
*May our intention equally extend to every being in place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to...*
